Variants.Content: Traveling City is a castle territory in the Riverlands famous for its roads and resting functions. The towns, inns, and ferries of the Riverlands are often better remembered than the mountain fortresses, because men, horses, goods, and messages had to stop here to change carriages, drink water, or wait for the water to drop. The value of Travelodge lies in these ordinary pauses: it can collect revenue from road traffic, but it must also face bandits, rumors, and diseases brought by the gathering of strangers. The Riverlands are both fertile and have no natural barriers, making it difficult for Travelodge to remain completely isolated.

Entry Wayfarer's Rest Local families also relied on river transportation, ferries, wheat fields, mills, and hiding places when war came; if any road, well, spring, or dock failed, the price would fall first on them.

Entry Wayfarer's Rest They also recognize the accents, laws, and credentials of the Riverlands; reputations can travel great distances from taverns, but true distances must still be measured by wheel, oar, or horse's hooves.
Entry Wayfarer's Rest Entry Wayfarer's Rest

Entry Wayfarer's Rest If you can supply supplies, avoid danger, and find a guide, it is worth marking in your itinerary; if you don't have these three things, no matter how loud your family name is, it won't be able to save the lost.

From workshops to sanctuaries, Travel's Rest juxtaposes quarrying, logging, ironwork, goat hair, and wall foundations built against the mountains with memories of the Seven Gods, ancient legends of river kings, and the land that changed hands over and over again. A stronghold was therefore not just a lord's hall, but also a place where weddings and funerals, vows, labor and local memories recurred.

Entry Wayfarer's Rest They care about river transportation, ferries, wheat fields, mills, and hiding places when war comes. They also care about whether seeds are left after collecting grain and whether the city gates are open in times of disaster. When people from afar see coats of arms, what they see is whether there will be food to eat tomorrow.
